{"id": "bd509a82-6d0c-4ded-b33d-fc7c45418e9b", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_QXp7HbNUFhzGT6hxDLeX52", "content": "[{'text': '## Documentation search results\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Origin settings\",\"context\":\"## Connection timeout\\\\n\\\\nThe connection timeout is the number of seconds that CloudFront waits when trying to\\\\nestablish a connection to the origin. You can specify a number of seconds between 1 and\\\\n10 (inclusive). The default timeout (if you don\u2019t specify otherwise) is 10\\\\nseconds.\\\\n\\\\nUse this setting together with **Connection attempts** to specify how\\\\nlong CloudFront waits before attempting to connect to the secondary origin or before returning\\\\nan error response to the viewer. By default, CloudFront waits as long as 30 seconds (3\\\\nattempts of 10 seconds each) before attempting to connect to the secondary origin or\\\\nreturning an error response. You can reduce this time by specifying fewer attempts, a\\\\nshorter connection timeout, or both.\\\\n\\\\nIf CloudFront doesn\u2019t establish a connection to the origin within the specified number of\\\\nseconds, CloudFront does one of the following:\\\\n\\\\n* If the specified number of **Connection attempts** is more\\\\n than 1, CloudFront tries again to establish a connection. CloudFront tries up to 3 times, as\\\\n determined by the value of **Connection attempts**.\\\\n* If all the connection attempts fail and the origin is part of an origin group,\\\\n CloudFront attempts to connect to the secondary origin. If the specified number of\\\\n connection attempts to the secondary origin fail, then CloudFront returns an error\\\\n response to the viewer.\\\\n* If all the connection attempts fail and the origin is not part of an origin\\\\n group, CloudFront returns an error response to the viewer\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistValuesOrigin.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"How do I increase the response and keep-alive timeout quotas for my CloudFront custom or VPC origin?\",\"context\":\"### Increase the response timeout and keep-alive settings for your CloudFront distribution\\\\n\\\\nTo increase how long CloudFront waits for a response from the origin, update the [response timeout](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistValuesOrigin.html#DownloadDistValuesOriginResponseTimeout) value. The default value is 120 seconds, but you can request a higher quota increase up to 180 seconds.\\\\n\\\\nTo maintain a longer connection to your custom origin after it gets the last response packet, increase the [keep-alive timeout](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/DownloadDistValuesOrigin.html#DownloadDistValuesOriginKeepaliveTimeout) value. The default keep-alive timeout value is 5 seconds, but you can increase the timeout value up to 180 seconds.\\\\n\\\\nComplete the following steps:\\\\n\\\\n1. Open the [CloudFront console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudfront/).\\\\n2. In the navigation pane, choose **Distributions**, and then select your distribution.\\\\n3. Choose the **Origins** tab, and then select your origin.\\\\n4. Choose **Edit**, and then expand **Additional settings**.\\\\n5. For **Response timeout**, enter the new timeout value.\\\\n6. For **Keep-alive timeout**, enter the new timeout value.\\\\n7. Choose **Save changes**.\\\\n\\\\n**Important:** If you receive \\\\\"HTTP 504\\\\\" errors from CloudFront, then see [HTTP 504 status code (Gateway Timeout)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/http-504-gateway-timeout.html)\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/cloudfront-custom-origin-response\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Improve your website availability with Amazon CloudFront | Networking & Content Delivery\",\"context\":\"## Origin failover\\\\n\\\\nAmazon CloudFront provides origin server failover. This feature automatically routed to a pre-configured secondary origin server when the primary origin server is unavailable. By using this feature, even if the primary origin server goes down or enters an unstable condition, CloudFront switches to the pre-configured secondary origin to provide consistent user experience. CloudFront failover allows you to switch origin servers by triggering an origin application response code and timeouts. The result is that even if an application error is caused by unexpected factors, your application will continue without interruption.\\\\n\\\\nTo use the failover feature, create an origin group and specify the secondary origin so that CloudFront automatically switches to it when it receives an error response with a specific HTTP status code from the primary origin. The two origins in the origin group can be any combination of Amazon S3 buckets or custom origin. CloudFront fails over to the secondary origin \u2014 when the HTTP method of the viewer request is GET, HEAD, or OPTIONS \u2014 if the primary origin returns one of the specified error status codes, or if the connection to the primary origin fails or experiences a timeout.\\\\n\\\\nTimeout settings that trigger origin failover include the following (June 2020 update now provides extended timeout settings).\\\\n\\\\n* Origin Connection Attempts: Number of attempts to connect to the origin (can be changed in the range of 1-3 times)\\\\n* Origin Connection Timeout: The amount of time to wait when establishing a connection to the origin (can be changed in the range of 1-10 seconds)\\\\n* Origin Response Timeout: The amount of time to wait for a response from the origin (can be changed in the range of 1-60 seconds. \u2013 applies only to custom origins)\\\\n\\\\nFor some use cases, like live streaming content, you might want CloudFront to fail over to the secondary origin more quickly, with fewer attempts, such as within the half-life of a video segment duration. For example, if your segments are 4 seconds, set the timeout to 2 seconds with no retries. Or for other use cases, like querying a database that takes long for processing, you might want a longer timeout value. You can adjust those values depending on the nature of your application or origin server\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/improve-your-website-availability-with-amazon-cloudfront/\"}]}}\\n\\n## Recent AWS announcements (What\\'s New)\\n\\nNewer than your training data may be. When these conflict with the documentation results above or with what you remember, prefer the most recent dated source.\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Amazon CloudFront introduces new origin response timeout controls - AWS\",\"context\":\"Amazon CloudFront has introduced two new capabilities to enhance origin timeout controls. The first is a response completion timeout, which allows users to configure the maximum amount of time CloudFront should wait for a complete response from their origin across all packets and retries. This is particularly useful for latency-sensitive workloads like media streaming or API calls. The second capability is the ability to set custom response timeout values for Amazon S3 origins instead of the default value of 30 seconds. These enhancements provide more granular control over origin response timeouts and enable consistent and reliable user experiences despite network conditions or origin performance. Both response completion timeout and custom response timeout values for Amazon S3 origins are supported across all CloudFront edge locations, excluding the AWS China (Beijing) region. Users can configure origin timeouts using the CloudFront console, API, and AWS CloudFormation at no additional charge\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/07/amazon-cloudfront-origin-response-timeout-controls/\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Configure Read Timeout and Keep-Alive Timeout values for your Amazon CloudFront Custom Origins\",\"context\":\"Amazon CloudFront, a content delivery network (CDN) service by AWS, has introduced the capability for users to configure read timeout and keep-alive timeout values for their custom origins. The read timeout value determines how long CloudFront waits for a response from the custom origin before considering it as a timeout\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2017/03/announcing-configure-read-timeout-and-keep-alive-timeout-values-for-your-amazon-cloudfront-custom-origins/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Amazon CloudFront now supports TLS 1.3 for origin connections - AWS\",\"context\":\"Amazon CloudFront has implemented support for Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 when connecting to origins, enhancing security and improving performance for origin communications. This upgrade offers stronger encryption algorithms, reduced handshake latency, and a better overall security posture for data transmission between CloudFront edge locations and origin servers. TLS 1.3 is automatically enabled for all origin types, including custom origins, Amazon S3, and Application Load Balancers, with no configuration changes required. TLS 1.3 provides faster connection establishment through a reduced number of round trips during the handshake process, delivering up to 30% improvement in connection performance when the origin supports it. CloudFront will automatically negotiate TLS 1.3 when the origin supports it, while maintaining backward compatibility with lower TLS versions for origins that haven\\'t yet upgraded. This enhancement benefits applications requiring high security standards, such as financial services, healthcare, and e-commerce platforms that handle sensitive data. TLS 1.3 support for origin connections is available at no additional charge in all CloudFront edge locations. For more information about CloudFront origin TLS, refer to the Amazon CloudFront Developer Guide\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2025/11/amazon-cloudfront-tls13-origin/\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"Amazon CloudFront announces mutual TLS support for origins - AWS\",\"context\":\"Amazon CloudFront has introduced mutual TLS (mTLS) support for origins, allowing customers to authenticate requests from their CloudFront distributions to origin servers using TLS certificates. This eliminates the need for custom security controls and reduces operational overhead. Origin mTLS is supported for origins on AWS, such as Application Load Balancer and API Gateway, as well as on-premises and custom origins. Customers can use certificates issued by AWS Private Certificate Authority or third-party private Certificate Authorities, which they import through AWS Certificate Manager. Origin mTLS is available at no extra cost and is supported in the Business and Premium pricing plans. Customers can configure origin mTLS using various methods, including the AWS Management Console, CLI, SDK, CDK, or CloudFormation. Origin mTLS provides cryptographic verification of CloudFront\\'s identity and ensures that only verified CloudFront distributions can connect to backend infrastructure\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2026/01/amazon-cloudfront-mutual-tls-for-origins/\"},{\"rank_order\":5,\"title\":\"cloudfront\",\"skill_description\":\"Configures Amazon CloudFront content delivery across six workflows: when to use CloudFront and how it fits with AWS WAF, Shield, CloudFront Functions, Lambda@Edge, Route 53, and origins (creating a distribution, caching, and Flat Rate Pricing (FRP) versus pay-as-you-go pricing); managing custom-domain TLS certificates (ACM in us-east-1); configuring multi-tenant distributions; protecting origins with origin access control (OAC), VPC origins, and origin mutual TLS (mTLS); securing content with signed URLs and cookies, geographic restrictions, viewer mutual TLS, and edge token validation; and observing traffic with standard and real-time logs. Applicable when the customer wants to put CloudFront in front of content, choose pricing, lock an origin, restrict who can view content, or analyze logs. Not applicable for the Route 53 DNS side of a CloudFront custom domain or failover between distributions, or for pure-Route 53 DNS work (see the route53 skill).\\\\n\\\\n\\\\nServices: cloudfront, s3, acm, vpc\\\\nTasks: configure, secure, deploy\\\\nPersona: developer, devops, sre\\\\nWorkload: networking, content-delivery, security\",\"skill_name\":\"cloudfront\"}]}}'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "2aa70a91-8e7c-4795-96c1-6e43fd4d03b9", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Using CloudFront's default origin settings isn't automatically a fail — but whether it "passes" an operational review depends on what the review is actually checking for. Here's the breakdown:

**The defaults themselves:**
- **Connection attempts:** 3 (range 1–3)
- **Connection timeout:** 10 seconds (range 1–10)
- **Response timeout:** 30 seconds by default for custom origins (S3 origins now also support a customizable value instead of the fixed 30s)

Combined, that means CloudFront can wait up to ~30 seconds (3 × 10s) just trying to establish a connection before failing over or returning an error to the viewer, plus the response timeout on top of that.

**Why a reviewer might flag defaults:**
- For latency-sensitive workloads (live/video streaming, real-time APIs), AWS's own guidance recommends *tuning these down* — fewer attempts and shorter timeouts — so CloudFront fails over to a secondary origin or returns an error faster, rather than leaving viewers waiting up to 30+ seconds.
- If you have an origin group configured for failover, defaults can significantly delay failover kicking in.
- If your origin is known to be slow (e.g., long-processing backend/database queries), a longer response timeout than default might actually be *more* appropriate — so "default" could be wrong in the other direction too.

**Why defaults might be fine:**
- For typical web content delivery without strict latency SLAs or without an origin group, the defaults are reasonable and commonly used — nothing inherently insecure or broken about them.

So there's no blanket pass/fail rule tied to "used the default" alone — it comes down to whether the defaults match your workload's failover/latency requirements. If you want, I can check your actual distributions and origins to see if any have failover groups or latency-sensitive use cases where the defaults would be worth tuning.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
